questions.q: Who was E.M. Forster and what is the source of the essay "The Story" in Woven Words?
questions.a: E.M. Forster (1879–1970) was an English novelist, short story writer, and critic, best known for novels like A Passage to India and Howards End. The essay "The Story" is an excerpt from Chapter 2 of Aspects of the Novel, which originated as the Clark Lectures delivered at Trinity College, Cambridge, in spring 1927. A wrong answer (e.g., naming a different author or claiming it's a formal essay) reveals the student hasn't grasped the text's conversational, lecture-based nature, which explains its use of "I," "you," and informal phrasing.

questions.q: In your own words, explain what Forster means when he defines a story as "a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence" and why he calls it the "lowest and simplest of literary organisms."
questions.a: Forster means a story is just events in chronological order: dinner after breakfast, Tuesday after Monday, decay after death. It's the "lowest and simplest" because, qua story, it has only one merit (making us want to know what happens next) and one fault (failing to do so). It lacks the "finer growths" like character, value, or pattern. A wrong answer that equates "story" with "plot" or adds emotional depth shows the student hasn't separated the bare time-sequence from the novel's richer layers.

questions.q: Apply Forster's distinction between "life in time" and "life by values" to this sentence: "I only saw her for five minutes, but it was worth it." Identify which part reflects time and which reflects value.
questions.a: "Five minutes" reflects the life in time (chronological, measurable duration). "Worth it" reflects the life by values (intensity, significance, not measured in minutes). The sentence combines both allegiances. A wrong answer that treats both parts as time or both as value shows the student hasn't internalised Forster's double-allegiance concept, which is central to his argument about what novels add beyond mere story.

questions.q: Analyse how Forster uses the Scheherazade analogy to prove that suspense ("what happens next?") is the story's only literary tool that works on "tyrants and savages." What does this reveal about the story's primitive origins?
questions.a: Forster argues Scheherazade survived not through her "exquisite descriptions," "tolerant judgements," or "ingenious incidents" (the finer growths), but solely by stopping at dawn with the king "gaping"—wielding suspense. This reveals the story's origin in a "primitive audience of shock-heads" kept awake only by curiosity about the next event. A wrong answer focusing on Scheherazade's literary skill misses Forster's point: the story is atavistic, predating civilisation, and its power is pre-artistic.

questions.q: Evaluate Forster's claim that "it is never possible for a novelist to deny time inside the fabric of his novel" by considering Emily Brontë (Wuthering Heights), Sterne (Tristram Shandy), and Proust. Do their experiments with time contradict or confirm his thesis?
questions.a: They confirm it. Brontë "tried to hide" her clock, Sterne "turned it upside down," Proust "kept altering the hands"—but none denied time's existence; they only manipulated its presentation. The "thread of story" (the tape-worm) remains. A wrong answer claiming these authors "broke" time sequence shows the student confuses narrative technique (order, duration, frequency) with the ontological necessity of time-sequence as the story's backbone.

questions.q: Create a two-sentence "lecture-style" opening for an essay on "Character in the Novel" that mimics Forster's conversational tone (using "I," "you," "curiously enough," "so to speak") and sets up a three-voice structure like his opening on "What does a novel do?"
questions.a: Example: "If you ask a certain type of reader, 'What does a novel's character do?' they'll reply, 'Well—I don't know—seems a funny question—characters are just people, so to speak,' probably scrolling their phone at the same time. Another, on a tennis court, will be brisk: 'What do they do? They act, of course, and I've no use for them if they don't. Give me a character who does something!' Curiously enough, a third voice—my own—says in a drooping tone, 'Yes—oh dear yes—characters act.'" A poor answer uses formal academic language, missing the "backwaters and shallows" style Forster defends.
